newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kinkel visits Moscow for talks on NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel visits Moscow for talks on NATO expansion.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel leaves for Moscow on Tuesday for talks with his Russian counterpart, Yevgeny Primakov, in the latest diplomatic effort to persuade Moscow to accept NATO's plan to expand eastward.
Kinkel was likely to meet top Russian officials and parliamentarians to discuss other security issues and some bilaterial issues, a foreign ministry spokesman said.

His main task would be to try to make the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's plans to take in former Communist-ruled countries from eastern Europe more palatable to Moscow, which has so far been virulently opposed to the idea.

"We will discuss...everything from the disarmament process to the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons on any new NATO territory -- something we have already pledged," Kinkel told the General Anzeiger daily newspaper in an interview.
"The Russian president (Boris Yeltsin) has difficulty justifying NATO expansion to the military and above all the intelligentsia at home. We have to help him in this," he said.
"I expect that we will reach a solution by the Madrid NATO summit in June. But this is not going to be easy," Kinkel said, adding that he was nevertheless optimistic.

On Monday Kinkel meets new U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in Bonn. Their talks were likely to focus on alliance proposals for a charter with Russia that envisages a joint council for intensive consultations.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Yeltsin's closest ally in the West, and other leaders have said Russia cannot veto NATO's enlargement, but they hope to reach an agreement with Russia on the expansion proposals.
German experts say Kinkel will probably discuss Yeltsin's proposal for a meeting in April to prepare for the June summit, when potential new members are expected to be invited to join.

"Obviously they are considering a meeting, at which nothing will be decided, but which should promote progress towards NATO expansion while many details still need to be hammered out," commented the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung daily newspaper.
The first countries likely to be enlisted are Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
French President Jacques Chirac and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi have been positive about the idea, but Kohl has declined say whether such a meeting was likely to take place.

Moscow's campaign against NATO's eastward expansion hit a new peak last week when one official said Moscow should be ready to use nuclear weapons if attacked with conventional arms. The Kremlin later distanced itself from his comments.

Russian officials demanded the right of veto on major European security issues and Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky warned NATO not to offer membership to the three Baltic states on Russia's northwestern border.

They also criticised NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana last week when he visited four former Soviet republics with which Moscow is trying to strengthen ties and accused the alliance of pursuing a covert anti-Moscow policy.

Kinkel's visit coincides with the latest in a flurry of top level contacts between NATO member states and Russia. It will also be the seventh meeting between Kinkel and Primakov in just under a year, the foreign ministry spokesman said on Friday.
Kohl met Yeltsin in Moscow last month. Afterwards he said he saw a chance for solving the differences with the Russians over NATO enlargement this year.
But later Yeltsin's spokesman said the Russian president had not softened his opposition to the alliance's expansion plans, dampening hopes in the alliance.
